key_terms.meaning: The part of a process's code that reads or writes a shared resource and must run alone.

Every process keeps a queue ordered by (timestamp, process id); a REQUEST with a timestamp goes to all, and a process enters when its request is first in the queue and it has a REPLY from every other process.

A process sends REQUEST(timestamp, id) to all and waits for n-1 REPLYs; a receiver replies at once unless it is inside the section or wants it with a lower timestamp, in which case it defers the reply.
A unique message carrying the right to enter the critical section; whoever holds it may enter.
The token carries a queue Q of waiting processes and an array LN of the last request number served for each process; every process keeps its own RN array of the largest request numbers it has seen.
RN[i] is the highest sequence number of the requests that process i has issued so far; it is compared with the token's array LN.
A directed graph with an edge from a waiting process to the process whose resource it waits for; a deadlock is a cycle in it.
A small control message (initiator, sender, receiver) that a site sends along wait-for edges to test whether a cycle passes through it.
A reported deadlock that does not really exist, caused by stale or in-transit state in a distributed wait-for graph.
Every correct process must decide one value: all decide the same value, and the value decided must be one that some process proposed.
In an asynchronous system with even one crash failure, no deterministic consensus algorithm is guaranteed to terminate.
A process that may behave arbitrarily or maliciously; tolerating f of them among n needs n ≥ 3f + 1.
A set with exactly one checkpoint per process and no message recorded as received but not as sent.
Cascading rollback in which one inconsistent checkpoint forces earlier and earlier checkpoints to be undone, sometimes to the start.
Several processes acting as one logical server so that the service survives the loss of a member.
The contract that fixes which value a read may return when the data sits on several replicas.
Reads and writes appear in one total order that respects each process's own program order.
A minimum set of replicas that must take part in an operation; with R + W > N, a read set and a write set always overlap.

takeaways: Mutual exclusion needs a total order; a timestamp pair (time, process id) supplies one with no central coordinator.
Timestamp algorithms spend 2(n-1) messages per entry and have a synchronization delay of one message time; Ricart-Agrawala removes the release message but still pays 2(n-1).
A token costs only 0 to n messages per entry but adds a wait of up to n message times when the token is elsewhere.
Deadlock detection in a distributed system can only chase cycles by passing probes; no site sees the whole wait-for graph.
Consensus is solvable only inside the limits set by the failure type (crash or Byzantine) and the timing model (synchronous or asynchronous).
A checkpoint set is usable only if it is globally consistent; otherwise recovery rolls back past consistent states.
Replication, reliable message delivery and consensus together turn unreliable processes and links into a service that keeps answering.
A consistency model is a trade: stricter models are easier to program against but cost more communication and latency.
bank_note: Examiners ask for comparisons backed by numbers: timestamp against token mutual exclusion, AND against OR deadlock models, and one consistency model against another, each supported by a worked trace and a message-complexity count.

bank.q: Describe Lamport's distributed mutual exclusion algorithm. Explain the three message types and prove that two processes can never be in the critical section together.
outline: State the queue of (timestamp, id) requests
REQUEST broadcast, REPLY unicast, RELEASE broadcast
Ordering rule: smaller timestamp wins, ties by process id
Proof uses total order of timestamps plus one REPLY held back per process
Message count 3(n-1) per entry

bank.q: Explain the Suzuki-Kasami token-based mutual exclusion algorithm. Give the data structures used at each process and the steps followed when the token arrives.
outline: Token holds Q and LN array; each site keeps RN
Requesting site increments RN[i] and broadcasts
Holder compares RN to LN and appends to Q
On release the holder updates LN and passes the token to the queue head
Message cost 0 to n per entry, delay up to n

bank.q: What are the AND and OR models of distributed deadlock? Explain the Chandy-Misra-Haas probe algorithm for each model.
outline: AND model: process needs all requested resources
OR model: process needs any one
Probe carries (initiator, sender, receiver)
Probe follows wait-for edges and returns to initiator to signal a cycle
Number of messages grows with edges, not with processes

bank.q: Define the consensus problem. Explain why the failure type and the timing model decide how many failures a system can survive.
outline: Agreement, validity, termination
Crash against Byzantine failures
Synchronous against asynchronous timing
Crash failures need 2f+1; Byzantine need 3f+1
FLP blocks guaranteed termination in asynchronous systems

bank.q: Explain checkpointing and rollback recovery. What is a globally consistent checkpoint set and what causes the domino effect?
outline: One local checkpoint per process
Consistency condition on in-transit messages
Recovery line and the domino effect
Coordinated checkpointing as a cure

bank.q: Three processes P1, P2, P3 have Lamport clocks 4, 4 and 2. P1 and P3 request the critical section at the same clock value from their own view. Trace Lamport's algorithm and state the order of entry.
outline: Form request tuples and sort by (timestamp, id)
Show queue contents at each stage
Show which replies are deferred
State the entry order and the release broadcasts

bank.q: Trace one full round of the Suzuki-Kasami algorithm for four processes when the token is held by P1 and P3 and P4 send requests with sequence numbers 2 and 5.
outline: Initial RN and LN values
Queue update on each request
Holder comparison of RN against LN
Token transfer order and final Q and LN
Message count for this round

bank.q: A distributed system has the waits P1 to P2, P2 to P3, P3 to P1, and P4 to P2. Run the Chandy-Misra-Haas OR-model probe algorithm from P1 and from P4 and state the result in each case.
outline: List the probes generated at each step
Show the probe that returns to its initiator
P1 reports a deadlock, P4 does not
Explain the difference between a cycle and a knot

bank.q: Compare Lamport's algorithm, Ricart-Agrawala and Suzuki-Kasami on messages per critical section entry, synchronization delay and throughput under heavy load. Show the cost figures for n = 5.
outline: 3(n-1) against 2(n-1) against 0 to n messages
Delay of one message time against up to n
Throughput under heavy load
Numerical table for n = 5
Which algorithm suits low load and which suits high load

bank.q: Explain the Byzantine generals problem. Show why n ≥ 3f + 1 is needed with oral messages and how signed messages relax the bound.
outline: Statement of the problem and the traitor count
Oral message algorithm OM(m) and its recursion
Bound 3f+1 with an f = 1 counterexample for n = 3
Signed messages allow n ≥ f + 2
Link to replicated services

bank.q: Compare coordinated checkpointing with message logging for rollback recovery. Which one avoids the domino effect and at what cost?
outline: Consistency requirement in each scheme
Coordinated checkpointing blocks or uses extra messages
Message logging keeps a volatile log and allows independent recovery
Domino effect ruled out by coordination and by logging
Cost in storage, blocking and recovery time

bank.q: Describe the consistency models from strict to eventual and explain which one a bank balance read in a UPI-style payment app needs.
outline: Strict, sequential, causal, eventual
Read-your-writes and monotonic reads
Quorum rule R + W > N
Balance check needs strong or linearizable read
Cost in latency and availability

bank.q: Explain how process groups, reliable message delivery and consensus work together to keep a replicated service alive when a process and some messages are lost.
outline: Flat and hierarchical groups
At-least-once and exactly-once delivery, retries and duplicate suppression
Agreement on the order of updates
Leader election after a crash
Failure masking seen by the client

glossary.def: The guarantee that at most one process at a time executes the code that touches a shared resource.
A counter that only tracks the order of events, not real time, so that if a happens before b then the clock of a is smaller.
A pair (clock value, process id) that gives a total order over all events in the system.
The time between one process leaving the critical section and the next process entering it.
Circulating one permission message around the processes; only its holder may enter the critical section.
The ordered list of pending requests kept inside the token in a token-based algorithm.
A set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another, so none can proceed.
A set of processes in a wait-for graph from which every path leads back into the set, so all of them are deadlocked.
A control message that follows wait-for edges to look for a cycle that returns to its starting site.
A false deadlock report produced by state that was true at different times at different sites.
A property saying nothing bad happens, such as two processes never being in the critical section together.
A property saying something good eventually happens, such as every request eventually being granted.
A process stops and stays silent; other processes can detect the silence.
A process continues to run but sends wrong or conflicting information.
A minimum number of replicas that must participate so that any two quorums overlap.
A copy of the same data or service placed on another machine for availability and speed.
A saved local state of one process from which it can restart.
The most recent consistent set of checkpoints, one per process, used to restart the system.
Recording received messages so that a failed process can replay them instead of rolling everyone back.
Each operation appears to take effect at a single instant between its call and its return, consistent with real time.
Replicas may differ for a while, but if updates stop, all replicas converge to the same value.
Delivery of a message to every member of a group, with retries and duplicate suppression, despite losses.
A distributed global state recorded by sending markers along channels so that no site needs to stop the computation.
Choosing one process from a group to act on its behalf, and choosing another when it fails.
